title: Digital Finance, Mobile Money and Digital Public Infrastructure
summary: How mobile money, agent networks, digital identity and fast payment systems have transformed access, and the regulatory choices that enable them while managing new risks.
contentGaps: Written as part of a programme: Aim and Purpose is the module's one-line description; audience, prior knowledge and core reading come from the programme

sections.Aim and Purpose: How mobile money, agent networks, digital identity and fast payment systems have transformed access, and the regulatory choices that enable them while managing new risks.
Learning Objectives: Explain how digital financial services expand access
Assess enabling regulation for e-money, agents and digital credit
Evaluate the role of digital identity and proportionate customer due diligence
Syllabus: Mobile money, agent networks and interoperability
Digital credit, buy now pay later and over-indebtedness
Digital identity, tiered due diligence and FATF guidance on inclusion
Digital public infrastructure and government-to-person payments
Intended Audience: Officials in finance ministries, treasuries and central banks responsible for financial inclusion and consumer policy
Staff of consumer protection agencies, ombudsman schemes and financial education bodies
Legislative drafters, legal advisers and parliamentary committee staff working on consumer and financial inclusion legislation
sections.Useful Prior Knowledge and Experience: Some familiarity with financial services, social or consumer policy is helpful. No technical background in financial regulation is required.
Core Reading: G20/OECD (2022), High-Level Principles on Financial Consumer Protection
World Bank (2017), Good Practices for Financial Consumer Protection
OECD (2020), Recommendation of the Council on Financial Literacy
CPMI and World Bank (2016), Payment Aspects of Financial Inclusion
World Bank (2022), The Global Findex Database 2021: Financial Inclusion, Digital Payments, and Resilience in the Age of COVID-19
